operand.headline: Innocence Found
operand.dek: What we can learn from Nashville attorney Jason Gichner, Executive Director of Tennessee Innocence Project — and a round-up of recent developments in Tennessee's fight against wrongful conviction.

tokens.c: Joyce Watkins could have thrown her boyfriend Charlie Dunn under the bus when they were both on trial for first-degree murder in Nashville in 1988 when the DA asked her to testify against Charlie, but she chose not to.

q.web-mujdcohd0: The Dunn and Watkins family have been close since the beginning, but even closer since last month. That's when for the first time they heard Watkins was offered a deal to testify against Dunn and avoid prison. She declined. When asked why? She said, "because Charlie was innocent. We were innocent."

body.caption: Joyce Watkins, client of Tennessee Innocence Project, and Executive Director of TIP Jason Gichner at a court hearing.

tokens.c: Instead, the jury convicted Joyce and she received a life sentence in prison for a crime she did not commit.

q.web-mujdcolp0: Joyce and Charlie had no criminal records. They had cooperated fully with police, allowed investigators into their home, and brought the child in for medical attention themselves. None of it mattered. On August 5, 1988, a jury convicted them both of first-degree murder and aggravated rape. They were sentenced to life in prison.

tokens.c: Some 27 years later, the nonprofit legal organization Tennessee Innocence Project (TIP), working with the Davidson County DA’s Conviction Review Unit, made right what was so deeply wrong.

q.web-mujdcopz0: Watkins and the late Charlie Dunn were convicted in 1988 for the rape and murder of a 4 year old girl. A review of the case by the Conviction Review Unit in the Office of the District Attorney for Nashville and the Tennessee Innocence Project found faulty testimony from the then state medical examiner.

tokens.c: Joyce was proven “actually innocent,” exonerated by the facts, as experts determined the central argument in the case had no basis in forensic science.

q.web-mujdcolp0: What TIP found was a conviction built on a crumbling foundation. Dr. Harlan’s central argument on the timing of the injury had no basis in forensic science. TIP brought the case to the Davidson County District Attorney’s Conviction Review Unit (CRU). The CRU conducted an independent investigation and uncovered additional evidence of innocence..
q.web-mujeq1pe0: The Davidson County Criminal Court found that Ms. Watkins and Mr. Dunn were actually innocent and vacated their convictions in an order issued on January 6.

tokens.c: Joyce was paroled in 2015, but not exonerated until 2022.

q.web-mujdcolp0: Joyce Watkins was released from prison on October 15, 2015, after serving 27 years for a crime she didn’t commit. She is the first black woman to be exonerated in Tennessee.

tokens.c: During those years, Joyce was required to remain on the Tennessee sex offender registry, in the parole system and existing under significant restrictions.

q.web-mujdcohd0: A hearing was held on Wednesday at 9 a.m. where Judge Angelita Blackshear Dalton shared her official ruling to dismiss the charges against them. As a result, Watkins is no longer listed on Tennessee's Sex Offender Registry.

tokens.c: This all cost Joyce a quarter century of her life path, but she would not back down from the truth.

tokens: Joyce lost out on building a life during those years — spending time with her friends and family, continuing a career path, reaching milestones, and all the other things that might have been.

tokens.c: And if all of this wasn’t heartbreaking enough, the costs are so high.
The expenses associated with exonerating someone convicted of a life sentence are astronomical.

tokens: And, last but not least, the cost of housing a person in prison for 27 years to Tennessee’s taxpayers is utterly wasteful.

tokens.c: This is a story where everybody loses.

No doubt highly controversial and profitable private prison operator CoreCivic, headquartered in Brentwood, Tenn., which owns and/or operates private prisons in our state and across America – including ICE facilities – may be disappointed to hear this.

q.web-mujdcpom0: The federal government has signed a deal with the private prison firm CoreCivic Corp. to reopen a 1,033-bed prison in Leavenworth as part of a surge of contracts U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has issued without seeking competitive bids.

tokens: CoreCivic is paid by the taxpayers per prisoner. That helps CoreCivic executives to reportedly receive significant financial compensation for what should never be a matter of economics.

tokens.c: In the news this summer – outside prosecutors decided not to pursue charges against Nashvillian Calvin Atchison, who was charged with murder in 2021 of a Nashville woman killed in 2000 after an innocent man, Paul Shane Garrett, was wrongly convicted of the murder in 2004 and spent a decade in prison.

q.web-mujdcpxa0: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WTVF) — A special prosecutor dismissed a first-degree murder charge against Calvin Atchison on Thursday, telling the court they could no longer prove the case beyond a reasonable doubt.

tokens.c: In the meantime, former Nashville District Attorney Torry Johnson, as well as a surprisingly long list of professionals in the Nashville law and order system (former Police Chief Steve Anderson, Public Information Officers Don Aaron for MNPD and Susan Niland for the DA’s office at the time, and then-Deputy DA Tom Thurman) knew years ago that, very likely, the wrong person had been convicted, as detailed in numerous news reports and public court documents – including a court order.

q.web-muiofr080: Confronted with this problem, Johnson convened what Judge Fishburn describes as a “clandestine” meeting in 2011. Roland and Postiglione presented their findings of Garrett’s innocence to Johnson, MNPD Chief Steve Anderson, Deputy DA Tom Thurman and ADA Kathy Morante. The potential fallout from the case was serious enough that the public relations leaders for the police and district attorney’s office, Don Aaron and Susan Niland, also were there. If Roland was right and Garrett was not the killer, an innocent man had been in prison for almost a decade.

tokens.c: “The extent of the intentional wrongdoing on so many occasions and at all levels of local law enforcement is so flagrant a violation of fundamental fairness that such conduct should be considered a due process violation standing alone…” wrote Davidson County Criminal Court Judge Mark Fishburn (Ret.)

q.web-mujdcqac0: “Their intentional decisions were the act of cowards to hide the truth for fear of public humiliation and legal retribution that might arise if their wrongdoing saw the light of day,” Fishburn wrote in an extraordinary six-page opinion in December in the case of Calvin Atchison, the man police now say killed sex worker Velma Tharpe in 2000.

tokens.c: To his credit, MNPD Detective Michael Roland tried to take action on the issue and was prevented from doing so, according to Judge Fishburn’s order.

q.web-muiofr080: In 2011, two of MNPD’s top detectives, Mike Roland and Pat Postiglione, were investigating a set of cold cases involving sex workers who were murdered in the same period as Tharpe. In the process, they reviewed the case of Garrett, a tow truck driver who had pleaded guilty after sitting in jail during a two-year investigation. According to Roland, the Garrett file was a mess because of poor documentation, shaky informants, deceptive interviews and a pair of problematic officers at the center of the investigation.

tokens.c: Garrett, whom TIP counts among its exonerees, was cleared in 2021 after Roland and the DA’s Conviction Review Unit reopened the case.

tokens.c: Even more recently, Governor Bill Lee commuted the life sentence of prisoner and TIP client Thomas Clardy in August.

q.web-muiofr083: Gov. Lee commuted Clardy’s sentence on Aug. 27, 2026, as part of a group of 33 pardons, citing the support Clardy received and the circumstances surrounding his conviction and sentencing.

tokens.c: Clardy, who TIP says was wrongly convicted, was incarcerated for a murder at an auto body shop in Madison in 2005.
